name: Karl Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so you can give me your public answer and your private view. What fills your usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Karl, 43, a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes museum catalog software. I have a bachelor’s degree and can fix ordinary search and display faults, though tricky data rules go to a specialist. I start with a museum report that an object is missing from search, trace the record, and test a correction. I use AI now and then to suggest search terms after colleagues have tried it, but I check the original catalog entry myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is this job supporting at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Amira, works as a physiotherapist, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is high for the job, and we have about ten months of expenses saved. There are plenty of similar jobs nearby. We are comfortable, but the mortgage is a real monthly bill, not a line on a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AI Plateau leaves people checking what a museum object really is. A suggested search term can help, but it should not erase the old catalog description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel secure about work and money. Ten months saved and Amira’s clinic income mean an ordinary code setback would not threaten our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing search fixes against original catalog entries and use AI only for low-risk term suggestions. I’d keep transferring 500 into savings each month while both wages hold. In the first year I’d ask museum staff to sign off on changed descriptions before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own job. I would still be bothered if software quietly changed how an object is described.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which catalog mistake do you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A museum could not find a ceramic bowl because our search lost the older name. I restored the ceramic bowl’s old name and asked the curator to check the label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family spending change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Amira we can keep the children’s summer camp and still save. I would not use the reserve to buy a bigger house on the strength of one good year.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking museum records.
I would preserve **original descriptions** when search terms change.
think: I expect my **job and income** to remain secure.
Our **ten-month cushion** and clinic wage cover ordinary setbacks.
do: **Keep** checking search fixes against original catalog entries.
**Transfer** 500 monthly into savings while both wages hold.
**Request** museum sign-off before changed descriptions are released.
feel: **Calm** about work, with care for accurate object labels.
S0.quote: I restored the ceramic bowl’s old name and asked the curator to check the label.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** helps search but does not replace original records or curator review.
High pay, **ten months saved** and many nearby jobs make his current work and money secure.

steps.text: Check museum search fixes against originals; obtain staff sign-off before releasing changed descriptions
Transfer 500 monthly into savings while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will speed search code, catalog checks and visitor replies. I would ask museum staff to test new labels before management reduces the catalog team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my own role could shrink if software does the first fix and the first description. I have savings, but a missing museum contract could still cut my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d run the approved assistant against twenty catalog searches that once returned the wrong object. If a curator checks the results, I’d learn to review its labels during paid work time. In the first year, if our catalog posts are cut, I’d join the staff association meeting to ask for notice and paid transition time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, though I could absorb a gap. A faster search could make the museum catalog less trustworthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the curator need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the curator the bowl with its old and new names. A tool should not erase the name a family used when they gave it to the museum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the staff association?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the twenty cases and ask which errors the new speed target ignores. If management cuts posts anyway, I would bring the list to the association.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed search code, catalog checks and replies.
I would seek **museum testing** before catalog posts are reduced.
think: I worry my **hours could shrink** if AI drafts both fixes and descriptions.
I can absorb a gap, but losing the **museum contract** would hurt my pay.
do: **Test** the approved assistant against twenty old wrong-object searches.
**Learn** label review during paid time after curator-checked results.
**Join** the staff association meeting if catalog posts are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours despite substantial savings.
S1.quote: A faster search could make the museum catalog less trustworthy.
fieldNote: He accepts **curator-checked evidence** before learning a new label-review workflow.

steps.text: Learn approved label review during paid time after curator checks twenty searches
Join staff association meeting if catalog posts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches our catalog-code thinking work by 2028. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, so Amira’s physiotherapy may have more time than my screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect our firm could lose most catalog coding work, including my role. Ten months saved gives us time, but other software openings may vanish at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for written severance terms and ask our staff association to compare offers if cuts are announced. I’d hold the planned house-extension money in cash. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for actual local vacancies and eligible income help, without promising the children a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large loss of income before we know what happens to Amira’s hands-on work. Ten months of savings is a search window, not a replacement career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the extension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the extension can wait, while their school and clinic routines stay. I would not turn a construction plan into debt during a job shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the association actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association for a group meeting if several catalog workers face cuts. We could compare severance letters without anyone signing alone.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach catalog code before hands-on robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Amira’s **physical care work** may change later.
think: I expect **catalog coding** work, including my role, to shrink sharply.
Our **ten-month savings** cannot guarantee a new software job.
do: **Hold** the house-extension fund in cash instead of starting construction.
**Organise** an association meeting if several catalog workers face cuts.
**Apply** for actual local jobs and eligible income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected lost pay despite a long cash runway.
S2.quote: Ten months of savings is a search window, not a replacement career.
fieldNote: His **2028 code risk** precedes robots around 2031 that might affect hands-on physiotherapy.
The **association meeting** requires group cuts; jobs and public help remain conditional.

steps.text: Delay the house extension and keep its fund in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to record why catalog descriptions were chosen. Thinking AI reaches code in 2031, while hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer coding jobs, but a longer warning lets me learn how museums check the origin of an object. I cannot assume that work survives full thinking AI as a paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one approved morning monthly with a curator reviewing the source for an object description. I’d use the museum’s free catalog guide if the company refuses that time, and keep examples I can explain. In the first year after 2031, if coding work ends, I’d apply only for actual collections-support vacancies whose pay covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the code job, though I have room to learn before making a move. I would keep the extension fund as cash until a real role appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which object would you use to prove the new skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would choose the ceramic bowl and explain where its older name came from. If the curator corrects my source, I would keep that note rather than hide the mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy an expensive heritage certificate from savings without a vacancy requiring it. The museum’s free catalog guide and one reviewed example are enough to start.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to document catalog sources.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect **fewer coding jobs** despite five years of warning.
I cannot assume **collections support** remains paid after full thinking AI.
do: **Learn** source checks monthly if a curator morning is approved.
**Use** the free catalog guide if approved time is refused.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying collections jobs if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about future pay, with time and savings to test a skill.
S3.quote: The museum’s free catalog guide and one reviewed example are enough to start.
fieldNote: His **five-year plan** produces reviewed source examples without buying a speculative certificate.
The **curator morning** needs approval; a paid collections role needs a real vacancy and adequate wage.

steps.text: Review catalog sources monthly if curator morning approved; otherwise use free guide

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 leaves a decade to preserve catalog records and plan how jobs change. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; robots for hands-on work follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay to hold in the near term, though I want the museum contract and staffing numbers in writing. Ten months saved gives us a voice, not a reason to stop asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing search changes against original entries and save 500 monthly while both wages hold. I’d ask the staff association to review catalog staffing once a year. In the first year after 2036, if coding work ends, I’d search actual local openings before considering a move with the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long view, but my work and mortgage look secure for now. I would use the time to keep the source records readable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at an association review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the old-name search error to the association and ask whether the team still has time for curator review. AGI by 2036 should not mean silent catalog staffing cuts now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the house plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira and I would keep the same house until an actual offer covers another mortgage and school travel. We would not build the extension just because the AI date sounds distant.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the catalog-code work could go before Amira’s hands-on work changes. Written severance, paid time to learn collections sources and real openings would help. Ten months lets us search, but it does not promise my skills still sell.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the name attached to an old object when software fills the catalog. A family’s story can disappear from search without anyone deleting a file.

headlineQuote: A family’s story can disappear from search without anyone deleting a file.
portrait: Karl is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, high pay and ten months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for museum search terms and checks changes against original catalog entries.
His partner’s **physiotherapy** faces hands-on robots later than thinking AI reaches his coding work.
He seeks **curator-reviewed learning**, staff association input and real vacancies while keeping extension money in cash.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his catalog coding role before the family tests another source of income.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid source-learning time and actual openings would help.
